Mohenjo-daro. The largest city of the Indus Valley Civilization, flourishing from approximately 2600 to 1900 BCE in what is now Pakistan. Its rectilinear street grid, standardized weights and measures, public baths, and sophisticated drainage systems demonstrate urban planning that rivals or exceeds contemporary Bronze Age cities, though its written script remains undeciphered, leaving much of its society shrouded in mystery.

Located in the Sindh province of Pakistan on the right bank of the Indus River, Mohenjo-daro was first excavated in the 1920s by archaeologists Rakhal Das Banerjee and Daya Ram Sahni. The city covered approximately three hundred acres and housed an estimated forty thousand residents at its peak, making it one of the largest cities of the Bronze Age world.

The city is laid out on a regular grid pattern with streets running at right angles, suggesting centralized planning and strong civic authority. The site features a Great Bath—a large public pool with sophisticated brick construction and drainage, possibly used for ritual purification or public gatherings. Standardized weights, measures, and tools discovered throughout the city indicate a complex economy and possibly a merchant class, yet the site shows remarkably little evidence of monumental religious architecture or royal palaces.

A written script appears on seals and pottery throughout the city, but remains undeciphered, preventing direct knowledge of the civilization's language, religion, or political structure. The civilization declined and was abandoned around 1900 BCE, with causes debated among scholars—possibly environmental change, devastating floods, or the drying of the Ghaggar River to the east. Yet Mohenjo-daro remains one of the most significant examples of early urbanization and urban planning in human history.
